title: Area II review: Preflight Responsibilities
intro: These questions mix all four Tasks of Area II: preflight action and fuel, airworthiness and documents, required and inoperative equipment, and inspections, ADs and preventive maintenance. Many put two of them into one real trip, the way a reviewing instructor would ask.

questions.q: You take off on a personal night VFR trip at 2000, well after the end of evening civil twilight. With forecast winds it is 1 hour 50 minutes to your first stop, at 8.5 GPH normal cruise. On preflight the landing light doesn't work. The airplane has no MEL, and the equipment list, KOEL and ADs don't require the light. What is true, ignoring taxi and climb fuel?
options: You need at least 19.8 gal, and the flight can't go at night without a landing light
You need at least 22.0 gal, and the landing light can't be deferred for any night flight
You need at least 22.0 gal; the landing light is required at night only for hire, so it may be deferred under 91.213(d)
You need at least 15.6 gal, because the reserve counts only on the trip home
questions.why: Trip fuel is 1.833 hr x 8.5 GPH = 15.6 gal. At night the reserve is 45 minutes: 0.75 x 8.5 = 6.4 gal, so 15.6 + 6.4 = 22.0 gal [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]]. Night means after the end of evening civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]. The 19.8 gal answer uses the 30-minute day reserve. 91.205(c) requires an electric landing light at night only if the aircraft is operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(4)]], so with no other (d)(2) test requiring it, it may be deactivated, placarded and found not a hazard under 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)-(4)]].

questions.q: Day VFR. You plan a fuel stop at airport B, 1 hour 40 minutes away with forecast winds, then 1 hour 30 minutes on to your destination C. Normal cruise burn is 9 GPH. What is the least fuel you may begin the flight with, ignoring taxi and climb?
options: 15.0 gal
19.5 gal
21.8 gal
33.0 gal
questions.why: 91.151(a) counts the reserve from the first point of intended landing, which is B [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]]. 1.667 hr x 9 GPH = 15.0 gal, plus the day reserve of 0.5 hr x 9 = 4.5 gal, gives 19.5 gal [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(1)]]. 33.0 gal is (3.167 hr x 9) + 4.5, which plans the whole trip as if you would not stop. 21.8 gal uses the 45-minute night reserve. You still need the same check again before the leg from B to C, and your own margin on top [[30:39|RMH 5-1]].

questions.q: IFR to an airport with an RNAV approach. ETA is 1500. The TAF shows 3,000 ft broken and 6 SM until 1530, then 1,800 ft broken and 4 SM. It is 1 hour 50 minutes to the destination, 35 minutes from there to the alternate, at 10.5 GPH. What is the minimum fuel under 91.167?
options: 27.1 gal
25.4 gal
33.3 gal
30.6 gal
questions.why: The alternate leg can be left out only if the forecast shows at least a 2,000 ft ceiling and 3 SM from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the ETA [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(b)]]. Here the ceiling drops to 1,800 ft at 1530, inside that window, so the alternate fuel counts. (110 + 35 + 45 min) = 190 min = 3.167 hr x 10.5 GPH = 33.3 gal [[60:468|14 CFR 91.167(a)(1)]] [[60:469|14 CFR 91.167(a)(2)-(3)]]. 27.1 gal leaves out the alternate because the ETA weather looks good, and 25.4 gal forgets the 45 minutes after the alternate.

questions.q: Low on fuel after a long hold, you declare an emergency. To land sooner you turn toward the airport and descend without waiting for a clearance. You land safely. What do the rules require of you afterward?
options: Tell ATC about the deviation as soon as possible; a written report goes to the FAA only if it asks for one
Nothing: an emergency excuses every report
A written report to the FAA within 48 hours, in every case
A written report to the FAA within 10 days, because a 'minimum fuel' call should have come first
questions.why: In an emergency the PIC may deviate from any part 91 rule as far as needed [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(b)]]. A PIC who deviates from an ATC clearance in an emergency must tell ATC about it as soon as possible [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(c)]]. A written report is sent only on the Administrator's request [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3(c)]]. The 48-hour report is for a pilot given priority without deviating from a rule, and only if ATC asks [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123(d)]]. 'Minimum fuel' is an advisory, not a required first step: if you need priority, declare the emergency [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]].

questions.q: Your 1965 airplane was not type certificated with a flight manual and flew long before March 1, 1979. Its limitations are in placards, markings and an owner's manual. You plan a trip to a short grass strip. What takeoff and landing information does 91.103(b) require you to know?
options: None: 91.103(b) applies only to aircraft required to have an approved flight manual
Only the runway length, because there is no approved data to use
Only the information needed if the flight is not in the vicinity of an airport
Other reliable information for this airplane's performance at the expected airport elevation, runway slope, gross weight, wind and temperature, plus the runway lengths
questions.why: 21.5 requires an approved flight manual only for airplanes with no flight time before March 1, 1979 [[60:34|14 CFR 21.5(a)]], so this airplane is not one that must carry approved distance data. For any flight, 91.103(b) still asks for runway lengths, and for aircraft like this one, other reliable performance information for the expected elevation, slope, weight, wind and temperature [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. The 'not in the vicinity of an airport' wording belongs to paragraph (a), not (b). On grass, expect the numbers to grow: one PHAK landing table adds 20% for dry grass [[1:283|PHAK Figure 11-32]].

questions.q: At 0600 you get an outlook briefing for a VFR departure at 1300. At 1245 you are at the airplane, and nothing else has been checked. What should you do before you leave?
options: Get a standard or abbreviated briefing first; an outlook briefing is for planning only
Nothing: the outlook briefing covered the whole flight
Check only the destination METAR, since the forecasts are already in hand
Ask for another outlook briefing, because you are now within 6 hours
questions.why: An outlook briefing is for departures 6 or more hours away and is for planning purposes only. The AIM says to get a standard or abbreviated briefing before departure for adverse conditions, current conditions, updated forecasts, winds aloft and NOTAMs [[34:68|AIM 7-1-5d]]. An outlook at 1245 makes no sense, since departure is now only 15 minutes away. Under 91.103 you must know all available information about the flight [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103]].

questions.q: You rent a Cessna 172 from a new FBO. The logbooks show an autopilot installed last month and approved for return to service. The only weight and balance report in the POH is dated three years ago. What should you do?
options: Use the old report; an autopilot changes the weight too little to matter
Fly, but with one less passenger to be safe
Fly: weight and balance records are the owner's job, not the pilot's
Find the revised weight and balance record that goes with the installation and use it; the PIC must use the most current data
questions.why: When equipment is added, the new empty weight and empty-weight CG are recorded in the weight and balance record and the equipment list is updated [[22:17|W&B Handbook 1-3]] [[22:30|W&B Handbook 2-10]]. The PIC is responsible for using the most current weight and balance data [[22:18|W&B Handbook 1-4]]. A guess like dropping a passenger doesn't replace the numbers, and extra equipment has overloaded many aircraft [[22:17|W&B Handbook 1-3]]. Current weight and balance data belongs on board [[24:41|AFH 2-4]].

questions.q: Your friend owned his airplane alone and died six weeks ago. The registration certificate in the airplane shows an expiration date in 2031, and the annual is current. His family asks you to fly it to a buyer's airport. What is true?
options: You may fly it: the registration is good until 2031
You may not fly it: the registration ended 30 days after his death, and without registration the airworthiness certificate is not effective
You may fly it until 60 days after his death, while the estate returns the certificate
You may fly it with the family's written permission
questions.why: A registration certificate stays effective only until certain events, one of which is 30 days after the death of the holder [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(a)]]. The 60 days is the time the estate has to return the certificate, not extra flying time [[60:169|14 CFR 47.41(b)]]. No person may operate the airplane without an effective registration [[60:156|14 CFR 47.3(b)]] [[60:486|14 CFR 91.203(a)(2)]], and an airworthiness certificate is effective only as long as the aircraft is registered in the United States [[60:66|14 CFR 21.181(a)]].

questions.q: The last annual ran out at the end of last month. This week the IA's new entry says the airplane was inspected in accordance with an annual inspection and a dated list of discrepancies and unairworthy items, including a cracked engine mount, was given to the owner. What does this mean?
options: The annual is done, so the airplane may fly for 12 calendar months
The airplane may fly for 30 days while the owner orders parts
The airplane is not approved for return to service; it may not fly until the items are repaired and it is approved, and the owner keeps the list until then
The airplane may fly if a private pilot signs the list
questions.why: That wording is the 43.11 entry for an aircraft not approved for return to service [[60:134|14 CFR 43.11(a)]]. 91.409(a) needs an annual and approval for return to service by a person authorized by 43.7 [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]], and no one may operate an aircraft after maintenance until it is approved and the record entry is made [[60:521|14 CFR 91.407(a)]]. The owner keeps the list of defects until they are repaired and the aircraft is approved for return to service [[60:526|14 CFR 91.417(b)(3)]]. There is no 30-day grace period in these rules.

questions.q: On a rental, the AD status list shows a recurring AD inspection due at 3,250.0 hours. The airplane shows 3,256.0 hours and there is no newer entry. The FBO says, "ADs are the owner's job, not yours. Go fly." What is true?
options: Don't go: anyone who operates a product that doesn't meet an applicable AD is in violation, each time it is operated
Go: the 10-hour allowance covers the extra 6 hours
Go: the owner is primarily responsible for AD compliance, so the pilot can't be in violation
Go, as long as you write the overdue AD in the squawk sheet
questions.why: The owner or operator is primarily responsible for airworthiness, including part 39 [[60:520|14 CFR 91.403(a)]]. But anyone who operates a product that does not meet an applicable AD violates 39.7, and does so each time the aircraft is operated [[60:125|14 CFR 39.7]] [[60:125|14 CFR 39.9]]. The PIC also decides whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight [[60:436|14 CFR 91.7(b)]]. The 10-hour allowance is for the 100-hour inspection only; there is no provision to overfly an AD's hour limit unless the AD itself allows it [[1:242|PHAK 9-12]].

questions.q: A friend's airplane has a pink airworthiness certificate marked "Restricted." He says pink certificates don't need annual inspections. What is true?
options: He is right: no special airworthiness certificate needs an annual
He is right only if the airplane is under 12,500 pounds
He is wrong: a pink certificate means the standard certificate has expired
He is wrong: the 91.409(c) exceptions name experimental, light-sport, provisional and special flight permit certificates, not restricted, so 91.409(a) still applies
questions.why: Pink means a special airworthiness certificate. It is issued for primary, restricted and limited category aircraft, light-sport aircraft, provisional certificates, special flight permits and experimental aircraft [[1:73|PHAK 3-2]]. 91.409(c)(1) excepts from the annual and 100-hour rules only an aircraft with a special flight permit, a current experimental certificate, a light-sport special certificate or a provisional certificate [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(c)]]. Restricted is not on that list, so the annual rule of 91.409(a) applies [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]. Pink is a kind of certificate, not a sign that one has expired.

questions.q: Thirty minutes into a night VFR cross-country, the rotating beacon, your airplane's only anticollision light, fails. What may you do?
options: Finish the whole round trip, because it failed in flight
Continue to a stop where it can be repaired or replaced; before the next takeoff it must be fixed or properly deferred
Land at once at the nearest airport and stay there until daylight
Defer it under 91.213(d) while airborne and keep flying
questions.why: At night an anticollision light system is required on all U.S.-registered aircraft, and if any light of it fails, the flight may continue to a stop where repairs or replacement can be made [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]]. Deferrals are not for in-flight failures [[1:239|PHAK 9-9]]. Before the next takeoff, 91.213 applies again, and an item required by 91.205 for that flight can't be deferred under 91.213(d) [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. A night return with the beacon still dark would not meet 91.205(c).

questions.q: You fly a privately owned single-engine turboprop under part 91. It has no MEL. Before a day VFR trip, a cabin reading light is found inoperative. How may you legally go?
options: Placard the light inoperative and make a no-hazard determination under 91.213(d)
Just go: a cabin light isn't on the 91.205 list
Get a verbal OK from the Flight Standards office
Not under 91.213(d): repair it, or fly under an approved MEL with an LOA, or under a special flight permit
questions.why: 91.213(d) is only for the aircraft listed in (d)(1), which names non-turbine-powered airplanes [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(1)]]. Turbine-powered airplanes may not be operated under 91.213(d) [[58:23|AC 91-67A 4.1.2.2]]. With an inoperative item installed and no 91.213(d) relief, you may not take off unless an approved MEL and an LOA in the aircraft provide for it [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]], or you fly under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]]. Otherwise it gets fixed. 91.205 is not the test here, because the turboprop can't use (d) at all.

questions.q: You fly for a part 135 charter operator that has an approved MEL issued under part 135 for one of its piston singles. You are moving that airplane empty under part 91 to another base. A cabin speaker is inoperative. Which method must you use?
options: The operator's MEL, because a person authorized to use a part 135 MEL must use it to comply with 91.213
91.213(d), because this flight is under part 91
No deferral is possible on a part 91 flight
Either one, at the pilot's choice
questions.why: A person authorized to use an approved MEL issued for a specific aircraft under subpart K, part 121, 125 or 135 must use that MEL to comply with 91.213 [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(c)]]. 91.213(d) itself opens with "except for operations conducted in accordance with paragraph (a) or (c)" [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]]. So flying under part 91 doesn't let you switch to the no-MEL method. Follow every condition and limitation in the MEL [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)(5)]].

questions.q: In your 1978 single (no MEL), the stall warning horn doesn't work. A friend says, "It isn't on the 91.205 day VFR list, so placard it and go." What is the correct reasoning?
options: He is right: 91.205 is the complete list of required items
Stall warning devices can always be deferred because the airspeed indicator still works
91.205 is only one of four tests: you must also check the VFR-day type certification equipment, the equipment list or KOEL, and ADs; if any requires it, it can't be deferred
It can be deferred only by an A&P under an MEL
questions.why: Under 91.213(d)(2) an item can't be deferred if it is part of the VFR-day type certification equipment, marked required on the equipment list or the KOEL for the flight, required by 91.205 or another part 91 rule, or required by an AD [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)]]. The stall warning device is not on the 91.205(b) list [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]], and in its MEL discussion the PHAK names it as an example of an item not listed as deferrable, which must be repaired before departure [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. So only the other three tests can decide it here. If one of them requires it, repair it or fly under a special flight permit [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(e)]]. With no MEL and LOA, the MEL route is not open [[60:492|14 CFR 91.213(a)]].

questions.q: Your non-turbocharged piston single (no MEL) has an inoperative directional gyro. Tonight you plan a personal night VFR flight; tomorrow, an IFR trip. The equipment list marks the DG as standard, the KOEL requires it only for IFR, and no AD applies. What is true?
options: Neither flight may go; a gyro instrument can never be deferred
Tonight's flight needs a special flight permit because it is at night
Both flights may go if it is placarded, since only the KOEL matters
Tonight it may be deferred under 91.213(d) once removed or deactivated, placarded "Inoperative" and found not a hazard; tomorrow's IFR trip needs it repaired
questions.why: The DG is not on the day or night VFR lists [[60:486|14 CFR 91.205(b)]] [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]], and the equipment list, KOEL and ADs don't require it for VFR, so 91.213(d) can be used: remove or deactivate it, placard it "Inoperative," and make the no-hazard determination [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)-(4)]]. For IFR, 91.205(d) requires a gyroscopic direction indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(9)]], and an item the KOEL requires for a kind of operation can't be deferred for it [[58:9|AC 91-67A 1.8.9]]. If deactivation involves maintenance, part 43 applies [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(3)(ii)]].

questions.q: During the runup, your transponder fails its self-test and won't come back. Your VFR route enters Class C airspace about 20 minutes after takeoff. What do the rules allow?
options: You must ask ATC at least 1 hour before entering the Class C
Ask the ATC facility with jurisdiction for a deviation; for an inoperative transponder the request may be made at any time
Defer it under 91.213(d) and fly the planned route as normal
Nothing: an aircraft with an inoperative transponder may not fly at all
questions.why: The transponder is required in Class C airspace [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(b)]], so it is required by another part 91 rule for that flight and can't simply be deferred for it [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)(2)(iii)]]. ATC may authorize a deviation, requested from the facility with jurisdiction [[60:494|14 CFR 91.215(d)]]. To fly with an inoperative transponder to the destination or to a repair shop, the request may be made at any time; the 1-hour rule is for an aircraft not equipped with a transponder [[60:495|14 CFR 91.215(d)(2)-(3)]].

questions.q: An airplane's annual was done and entered as an annual at 1,640.0 hours. Since then it has flown only private flights. Now, at 1,731.5 hours, its owner, a CFI, wants to start giving paid lessons in it. How many more hours may it fly on paid lessons before it needs another annual or 100-hour?
options: 8.5 hours
None: a separate 100-hour must be done before the first paid lesson
18.5 hours, counting the 10-hour allowance
100 hours, starting from the first paid lesson
questions.why: 91.409(b) applies to flight instruction for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides, and it is met by an annual or a 100-hour within the preceding 100 hours of time in service [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. So the annual counts: 1,640.0 + 100 = 1,740.0 hours, and 1,740.0 - 1,731.5 = 8.5 hours left. The extra 10 hours may be used only while en route to a place where the inspection can be done, not for more lessons [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]].

questions.q: Before an IFR flight you tune the departure airport's VOT. The CDI centers with the OBS at 005° and a FROM flag. What is the result?
options: Within limits: the airborne limit of 6° applies to any VOR check
Within limits, since the needle is centered
Out of limits: with a VOT the OBS should read 180° FROM
Out of limits: with a VOT the OBS should read 0° FROM, and 5° is more than the 4° allowed
questions.why: With a VOT and the CDI centered, the OBS should read 0° with FROM, or 180° with TO [[33:70|AIM 1-1-4]]. 005° FROM is a 5° error. A test signal at the airport of intended departure allows plus or minus 4° [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(1)]]. The 6° limit is for airborne checkpoints and airway checks [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(b)(3)]]. Don't fly IFR using that VOR until it is fixed or checked within limits by another method [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]].

questions.q: You fly for a small part 135 charter company. On a day off, the owner asks you to change the spark plugs in one of the company's charter airplanes and sign the logbook, since you hold a commercial certificate. What is true?
options: You may not under 43.3(g): pilot preventive maintenance is not allowed on an aircraft used under part 135
You may, because a commercial certificate is above the private minimum
You may: spark plugs are on the preventive maintenance list
You may, if you sign as a commercial pilot rather than as a private pilot
questions.why: Cleaning or replacing spark plugs is on the appendix A list [[60:142|14 CFR part 43 app. A(c)(20)]]. But 43.3(g) lets a pilot do preventive maintenance only on an aircraft owned or operated by that pilot which is not used under part 121, 129 or 135 [[60:130|14 CFR 43.3(g)]]. The certificate level matters for signing off work you are allowed to do [[60:132|14 CFR 43.7(f)]], not for this limit. A mechanic should do it.

questions.q: Today is October 22, 2026. Tomorrow you fly IFR in your own Cessna. The records show: annual and ELT inspection March 10, 2026; altimeter, static and encoder test and transponder test January 2025; last VOR check September 20, 2026. The static system hasn't been opened. What must you take care of first?
options: The altimeter, static and encoder test
The transponder test
A VOR check, because tomorrow the last one will be 33 days old
Nothing: everything is current
questions.why: For IFR using the VOR system, the equipment must have been checked within the preceding 30 days [[60:470|14 CFR 91.171(a)]]. September 20 to October 23 is 33 days. The altimeter, static and encoder test and the transponder test are good for 24 calendar months [[60:524|14 CFR 91.411(a)(1)]] [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413(a)]], so January 2025 tests are still current in October 2026. The annual and ELT inspection are within 12 calendar months [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]] [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(d)]]. Log the new check with date, place, bearing error and signature [[60:471|14 CFR 91.171(d)]].

questions.q: Your airplane has an analog 121.5/243 MHz ELT. The manufacturer's screened-room test isn't available, so you must test it in the airplane on the ground. What does the AIM say?
options: Test it in flight so the signal reaches farther
Test it only during the first 5 minutes after any hour, for no more than three audible sweeps
Test it any time, as long as it runs less than 1 hour in total
Test it only after telling Flight Service, for up to 5 minutes
questions.why: When a screened room can't be used, analog 121.5/243 MHz ELTs should be tested only during the first 5 minutes after any hour, no longer than three audible sweeps. Tests outside that period are coordinated with the nearest FAA control tower, and airborne tests are not authorized [[34:31|AIM 6-2-4]]. The 1 hour figure is the battery rule: replace or recharge it after more than 1 cumulative hour of use [[60:489|14 CFR 91.207(c)]].

questions.q: Your annual was signed October 3, 2025. You plan to fly to a friend's airport on October 30, 2026 and return home on November 2. No other inspection is planned. What is true?
options: Both legs are fine: the annual is good for 13 months
Neither leg is legal: the annual ran out on October 3, 2026
Both legs are fine, because you may exceed the inspection by up to 10 hours to get home
The outbound leg is fine; the return is not, unless a new annual is done first or you fly home on a special flight permit with all due ADs done
questions.why: Within the preceding 12 calendar months runs from any day of a month to the last day of the same month the next year [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]] [[60:521|14 CFR 91.409(a)]]. So the annual is good through October 31, 2026: October 30 works, November 2 doesn't. An aircraft overdue for its annual may be flown to where it can be done only on a special flight permit, and all ADs that are due must be done first [[1:238|PHAK 9-8]]. The 10-hour allowance is for the 100-hour, not the annual [[60:522|14 CFR 91.409(b)]]. Application: plan the alternative now, as 91.103 asks for alternatives if the flight can't be completed: an IA at your friend's airport, or a shorter trip [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(a)]].
